'There's a new listing near the park,' said Asif. 'Two bedrooms, third floor.'
'Didn't we see one like that in March?' said Yash.
'This one has a nicer kitchen. Let's book a visit.'
'That would be our forty-first.'
'Forty-second, actually. I've been counting.'
'What about the flat in April, the one with the big window? What was wrong with it?'
'Nothing. But maybe there was something better.'
'Prices in that area have gone up since then. It costs more now.' Yash closed the laptop. 'And we're still looking.'
'So we lost money by being careful?'
'We lost it by never deciding.'

qa.q: What other approach could help them finally choose?

qa.a: Yash likely feels frustrated and worried about rising prices, shown by closing the laptop and pointing out the higher cost.

We started looking for a flat in January last year. By this January, Rohan and I had seen forty-three.
Every time one came close, I'd think, but what if there's a better one next week? The one in Baner had a small kitchen. The one in Aundh faced west. The one in Wakad was perfect, but I'd heard about a new project nearby and wanted to compare. We kept saying, "Let's see a few more."
My friend Jaya bought her flat in March after seeing six. I secretly thought she'd settled.
Then, this month, we went back to the Wakad building. The same size of flat now costs noticeably more. The builder shrugged. "Prices moved."
Rohan didn't say anything on the drive home. Neither did I.
Jaya's flat is lovely, by the way. She's been living in it for ten months.
— Deepika

qa.q: How many flats had Deepika and Rohan seen by this January?
How did Deepika feel on the drive home after hearing the new price?
qa.a: Deepika felt regretful and deflated, realising the endless search had cost them more than choosing a good-enough flat earlier.

qa.q: What else could Deepika and Rohan have done to stop searching?
qa.a: They could have set a rule to choose the first flat that met all their must-haves within budget, instead of always waiting for one more option.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her own quick decision now?
qa.a: Jaya likely feels content, having settled into a lovely home ten months ago without an endless search.

grounding: It shows a couple visiting dozens of properties for a year, always seeking one more option, until prices rise and the delay costs them more.

Estate agent's note — Neelam and Farhan, Hyderabad. Written by Elizabeth.

I first showed Neelam and Farhan a flat in February last year. I've now shown them thirty-eight.
They are thoughtful, careful people. Every time we found a good match, they asked to see "just a couple more". A flat in Kondapur met almost everything; Neelam worried the lift was slow. Another in Madhapur was ideal; Farhan wanted to wait for a new launch.
Last week they called me about the Kondapur building again. The same type of unit is now priced clearly higher than last spring. I watched Neelam's face fall when I told her. Farhan said quietly, "We could have been living there for a year."
I don't think they were wrong to be careful. But the search had no end point.
What I did next: I suggested they write their must-haves and a deadline, and choose the first flat that meets them.

qa.q: How many flats had the agent shown Neelam and Farhan?
How did Neelam feel when she heard the new Kondapur price?
qa.a: Neelam felt disappointed and regretful; Neelam's face fell on hearing the price had gone up.

qa.q: What else could Neelam and Farhan do now?
qa.a: They could write their must-haves and a deadline, and choose the first flat within budget that meets them.

qa.q: How does the long search look to the estate agent?
qa.a: The agent sees a careful couple whose search never ended, and feels they lost more by delaying than a good-enough choice would have cost.

grounding: It shows a couple visiting dozens of flats for a year, always seeking one more option, while prices rise and the delay costs them more.
